text: I’ll model the air domain directly: a 12 mm-high annular gap from radius 95 to 160 mm, with 36 constant-width (8 mm) radial vane solids removed. This produces 36 disconnected passage volumes sharing the same named boundary types. I’ll use conformal Gmsh tetrahedra for the coarse mesh after exporting the five stitched STL patches. First I’m checking the installed CAD/export interfaces needed for that construction.
The interface probe stopped at a nonexistent helper, so I’ll re-import everything in the next accepted cell and inspect the actual compound constructor plus the exporter.

I’ll now create the exact fluid solid in metres. Each vane cutter is a radial 8 mm-wide rectangular prism extending slightly beyond the annulus and gap, so its end caps cannot accidentally become fluid boundaries. I’ll classify the resulting faces by their actual surface geometry and print volume, areas, and passage count before any meshing.

The CAD result has exactly 36 passage solids and the expected five boundary groups. The small volume difference from the simple rectangular estimate comes from clipping each constant-width rectangular vane against circular radii. I’ll render the fluid passages from an oblique view to verify that the topology matches the intended radial channels.

The preview shows 36 open radial air wedges bounded by the two friction faces and vane sides, with inner and outer openings. I’ll now export the five named patches in one stitched tessellation, as required, using 0.25 mm chordal tolerance.

For volume meshing I’ll preserve the CAD passages by exporting the exact fluid compound to STEP, importing it into Gmsh’s OCC kernel, and assigning physical surface groups from analytic surface types. A 4 mm target tetrahedral size gives roughly three elements across the 12 mm gap—appropriate for the requested coarse-first check.

The coarse tetrahedralization itself succeeded, but Gmsh’s OCC bounding-box tolerance caused all 72 horizontal faces to be misclassified as vane planes, leaving the friction patches empty. I’ll correct this using each plane’s center-of-mass \(z\) (0, 6, or 12 mm), regenerate the same coarse mesh, and then convert it to OpenFOAM.

The corrected grouping is now right (36 upper, 36 lower, 72 vane, 36 inlet, 36 outlet faces), but OpenFOAM conversion requires a minimal `system/controlDict`. Because the prior cell ended in error, I’ll repeat the corrected mesh generation in a self-contained accepted cell, create only that required case metadata, and convert.

The converted OpenFOAM mesh contains 30,237 tetrahedra and exactly the five requested boundary patches; Gmsh’s “undefined faces” are the internal tetrahedron faces and do not create a `defaultFaces` boundary patch. I’ll now run the binding `checkMesh` and inspect connected regions and geometric quality.

`checkMesh` reached the mesh but this OpenFOAM build also expects a minimal `fvSchemes` dictionary even for mesh checking. I’ll add standard mesh-only scheme entries and rerun the same bare check; no solver fields or boundary conditions are being created.
This build likewise requires `fvSolution` at startup. I’ll create both minimal dictionaries self-contained and run the binding check again.

The bare check passes and correctly reports 36 disconnected regions—one per sealed radial passage—with total mesh volume \(4.00164\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^3}\), close to the CAD volume. Because plate thickness does not enter the fluid volume, I’ll nevertheless create a companion rotor-solid STEP (not used for meshing) to explicitly preserve and measure the requested two 10 mm friction plates, 12 mm apart.

I’ll run the optional extended geometry diagnostics once for reference. This is not the acceptance bar, but it records determinant, interpolation-weight, concavity, and face-tet information for the tetrahedral mesh.
The extended check flags one of its additional criteria, so I’ll extract that exact diagnostic rather than infer it; the bare acceptance check remains `Mesh OK`.

The extended-only failure is 3,097 tetrahedra below its determinant threshold; all face tets, concavity, interpolation weights, volume ratios, and the entire bare `checkMesh` pass. This is recorded as a reference diagnostic rather than treated as a binding defect. I’ll now run the completion gate with no predicted advisory waivers.

The gate only warns that the STL manifest has no `location_in_mesh`. That point is unnecessary here because the volume mesh was generated directly from the 36 OCC CAD solids with Gmsh, not selected by `snappyHexMesh`; I’ll waive that inapplicable check explicitly.
